article.body:
Do you know where the first yeshiva outside of Eretz Yisroel was built? That’s right—in Mitzrayim! Yaakov Avinu sent Yehuda ahead of everyone else so he could set up a yeshiva in Mitzrayim.

Wait a second. Isn’t it strange that Yaakov needed to send Yehuda for this job if Yosef was already there? Yosef was a big talmid chacham and a great tzaddik! Why couldn’t Yosef set up the yeshiva?

The answer is that there’s a big difference between Yosef’s avodah and the avodah of Yehuda (who represents the other brothers). Yehuda and the other shevatim worked as shepherds; they spent most of their time studying Torah in the fields, staying away from gashmiyus.

Yosef, on the other hand, was different. He had a special mission from Hashem to rule over Mitzrayim, and needed to be involved with the gashmiyus details of running the country. Yosef did it all while remaining totally connected to Hashem. Still, in order to do his job properly, he couldn’t spend a lot of time studying Torah like Yehuda and the other shevatim.

So when the time came to start a yeshiva, Yaakov sent Yehuda, whose shlichus in life was to be completely focused on limmud Torah.

And [Yaakov] sent Yehuda before him...

Chayolim, at this time in our lives, our shlichus from Hashem is to study Torah like Yehuda. This must be our total focus!

Being a truly committed student also includes teaching Torah and mitzvos to others, because it helps strengthen limmud Torah in the world.

Through fulfilling our shlichus of limmud Torah and teaching others, we chayolim will bring Moshiach!

Where must every chayol put his/her focus?

Evenly divided for all types of avodah.

What kind of jobs today are similar to shepherding, the job of Yehuda and the other shevatim?

Which part of Torah do you feel especially enjoy learning?

Take a moment to think of everyday activities that distract you from your true shlichus in life. How can you help yourself to remain focused?

As kids, Torah is our whole avoda! Gather your group into two teams for this Torah-themed Scattergories game. Choose a letter of the alef-beis at random. Think of a word starting with that letter that fits each of the categories below. Each team has one minute to jot down as many answers as possible. You earn a point for every answer that the other team didn’t have. Don’t peek at the categories until you’re ready to play!

• Places mentioned in Tanach

• Names of people in Tanach

• Last name of a rabbi/ teacher

Write the first letter of each image on the blank line to guess

The avoda of Yosef and Yehuda are so different from each other! In each row, can you find the one that doesn’t belong?

On Asara B’Teves, we remember when Yerushalayim was surrounded by the army of Bavel. This eventually led to the churban. We also think about how we can help bring the Geulah.

and use the everyday things we do (like eating, playing, and learning) for Hashem, we bring more holiness into the world. Every time we jump to help another Yid do a mitzvah, Hashem joins us, and “jumps” to turn these sad times into times of joy.

The Seventy-Two Rooms 8 Teves, 3515 (Just over 100 years before the Chanuka miracle)

It’s Asara B’Teves. Everyone bends over their siddurim, saying selichos in low, serious voices. Line by line, they remember the tragedies that happened to the Yidden in the month of Teves.

write the Torah in Greek.”

When was the Torah translated to Greek? And why is that sad enough to mention in selichos?

*** More than two thousand years ago, the powerful King Talmai (Ptolemy) ruled over Mitzrayim and Yavan (Greece).

He had wealth, power, and a vast empire. But what he loved most was his enormous library, filled with books and scrolls from around the world.

Yet, one book was missing: the Torah.

“I want the Torah in my library,” King Talmai declared. “But it’s in Hebrew, and I can’t understand it. I must have it translated into Greek!”

When a king gives an order, no one dares to refuse. “Guards!” he commanded. “Bring me seventy-two of the greatest Jewish sages!”

The officers hurried to obey. Soon, seventy-two talmidei chachamim stood before the king.

But King Talmai didn’t tell them why they had been brought there. Before they could speak to one another, he sent each talmid chacham into a separate room. Then, going from room to room, he gave them all the same command: “Translate the Torah into Greek!”

The doors closed, and each sage began to write.

But soon, they all realized the same problem: In thirteen places, a correct translation could cause King Talmai to misunderstand the Torah. They would have to change the words to express the Torah's true meaning.

But what if each talmid chacham made different changes? What if the translations didn’t match? King Talmai would be furious!

There was no way to know what the others were writing. They each had to decide on their own.

Finally, on Ches Teves, the translations were finished.

“Lay out the scrolls and compare them!” King Talmai ordered.

The guards obeyed. To the chachamim's amazement, every translation was identical. All seventy-two chachamim had made the exact same thirteen changes!

But surprisingly, the chachamim didn't celebrate. They saw this as one of the saddest days in Jewish history—as tragic as the day the Yidden made the Eigel Hazahav.

Why? After such a great neis, what was so sad?

Chazal didn’t compare the translation to bowing to the Eigel. They compared it to the day that the Eigel was made.

On that day, no one had worshipped it yet. But what had been created? The possibility for the aveira to happen later.

The same was true on Ches Teves. The chachamim had translated the Torah carefully, and Hashem even made a neis to protect them.

But still, they saw what could happen later. Now that the Torah was available in Greek, anyone could learn it anywhere. Instead of being taught in an environment of warmth and kedusha by teachers with Yiras Shamayim, it could be misunderstood and even misused. This possibility is what made Ches Teves such a sad day.

We can learn from this, too. Sometimes, things seem fine at first—a new book, an exciting game, a funny comment.

But a Yid stops and thinks: Where could this lead? Will it still be good later?
